x1a8uyli.author: Aristotle
x1a8uyli.label: Character from habit; the lawgiver habituates
x1a8uyli.translation: whereas the Moral comes from custom, and so the Greek term denoting it is but a slight deflection from the term denoting custom in that language. ... because the law-givers make the individual members good men by habituation, and this is the intention certainly of every law-giver,
x1a8uyli.translator: D. P. Chase (1847; Everyman edition); Greek: I. Bywater (1894)
x1a8uyli.reading: Responsibility falls first on the polity, because the lawgiver is not a bureaucrat but an ἠθοπλάστης, a shaper of character: law habituates (ἐθίζει) and so "initiates" the soul into values. Good laws, she says, are ones citizens can fall in love with.

x1rzy1.author: Plato
x1rzy1.label: Arete: the ever-flowing soul
x1rzy1.translation: arete will be the opposite of it, signifying in the first place ease of motion, then that the stream of the good soul is unimpeded, and has therefore the attribute of ever flowing without let or hindrance, and is therefore called arete, or, more correctly, aeireite (ever-flowing),
